title: Kaliya's Wives Plead for His Life
story:
The serpent lay still at the edge of the dark pool, his many heads drooping and torn where the boy's feet had come down on them, and for a long moment it seemed even the river held its breath. Kaliya, whose poison had made the Yamuna unfit to drink, was broken at last.

Then, from the far side of the water, his wives came forward. Their hair was loose and their garments had slipped from their shoulders, and they carried their little children close against them as they waded through the mud. One by one they lowered themselves to the ground and laid their bodies before Krishna, hands folded, and they did not ask to be spared. They asked that their husband be.

“The punishment is just,” they said. “Our husband is an offender, and your coming into the world is to subdue the wicked. Yet you look with equal eyes upon the children even of your own enemies, and what you give as punishment comes back to us as grace.” Even the blow that had fallen on the proud serpent, they said, was itself a blessing, for it was washing the stain from him.

Then their praise rose through the evening air like the smoke of an offering. They called Krishna by the oldest names they knew — the great Soul, the storehouse of knowledge and wisdom, the Infinite One of unbroken power. They called him Time, the navel of time, the witness who watches over every part of it, and the Self who stands behind the elements and the senses, the breath, the mind, the heart. Homage, they said, to the subtle one, the unchanging one, the seer, the source from which every scripture flows. Homage to Krishna, to Rama, to the son of Vasudeva. He was the lamp that lights the strands of the world and the one who hides them again; his play lay beyond all that is made, and yet through him everything made came to be. Though he himself desired nothing, all the powers of action and of time were held in him. He knew the highest and the lowest, and he stood over it all, keeping watch.

All the beings of the three worlds, they told him — the peaceful, the restless, the bewildered — were only his forms; but it was the peaceful who were dear to him, and it was to guard them and to hold up what is right that he had come at all.

Then they came to the heart of it, and their voices dropped. “A wrong done once by a husband,” they said, “should be borne with, as one bears with the wrongs of one's own children.” They looked at the great serpent lying still, and at the boy standing on the water. “Grant us your favour, Lord. The serpent is giving up his life. Tell us, your servants, what we are to do.”

They had not come to argue that Kaliya was innocent, nor with anger or threats or bargaining. They had come with their children and their loosened hair and their folded hands, and they had laid between the boy and the dying king of serpents the one thing no one had offered Kaliya before — a word spoken on his behalf.

Krishna listened.
reflection: The wives never argue Kaliya's innocence. They accept the punishment as just, then turn that acceptance into their plea — the blow itself, they say, is grace. Their intercession works because it asks for nothing on the serpent's merits, only on Krishna's own evenness of eye.
content_note: Kaliya is shown beaten and near death after Krishna's dance on his heads.
next_story_tease: But the serpent's life still hung upon Krishna's answer.
hero_scene: The wives of Kaliya kneeling before Krishna on the riverbank at dusk, their hair loose and their garments slipping, hands folded, little children pressed close, as the great serpent lies broken in the water behind them.
visual_elements: the broken serpent in the pool
